speaker: Unknown
en: You can't just nestle this under an existing business unit.

speaker: Unknown
en: It has to have its own kind of independence.

speaker: Unknown

speaker: Unknown
en: What are some patterns of where the best ideas come from?

speaker: Unknown
en: They don't come in conventional places.

speaker: Unknown

zh: 我现在实际上很看重看人的一点是：他们的「反学习率」是多少？

speaker: Unknown

zh: 他们能多快学会一样东西，然后又能放得下它？

speaker: Unknown
en: When you're showing people early prototypes, you're looking at people's eyes.
zh: 当你向人们展示早期原型时，你看的是人们的眼睛。

speaker: Unknown
en: That is the metric.
zh: 那就是指标。

speaker: Unknown
en: What are signs that it's time to kill an idea?
zh: 有哪些迹象表明是时候砍掉一个想法了？

speaker: Unknown
en: The team usually knows before the leader knows.
zh: 团队通常比领导者更早知道。

speaker: Unknown
en: Today my guest is Josh Woodward.

speaker: Unknown

speaker: Unknown
en: He's been at Google for over 16 years and his job is to experiment with and scale new AI products.
zh: 他在 Google 待了超过 16 年，他的工作是试验并扩展新的 AI 产品。

speaker: Unknown
en: My premise for this conversation and why I believe it is so valuable is that every company is being forced to think and operate like a Labs team because what is now possible is changing so quickly, you have to get very good at playing with the latest technologies, running tons of experiments, and uncovering new opportunities before your competition or startups do.

speaker: Unknown

zh: Josh 运营着世界上存续时间最长、规模最大的 Labs 团队，他分享了大量非常具体的经验：最好的想法来自哪里、如何知道什么时候该放弃一个想法、拥有产品市场契合度时是什么样子、在当今时代哪些技能正变得更值钱、为什么角色其实并没有模糊成一个单一的建设者角色等等，还包括一些劲爆的内容。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so it feels like the skills that will matter more and more now are things that you all have gotten really good at, which is finding great ideas, figuring out how to run a ton of experiments, figuring out what to double down on, building teams that can operate this way, at the same time not distracting the rest of the company from all the shiny stuff and letting them focus.

speaker: Unknown
en: So I'm going to start with coming up with ideas, finding great ideas.
zh: 那么我想从想点子、找到好点子开始。

speaker: Unknown
en: If you were to reflect back on the best ideas that emerged out of Labs and even in Google in general, what are some patterns of where the best ideas come from?
zh: 如果你回顾一下 Labs 乃至整个 Google 诞生过的最好点子，最好的点子来自哪些地方，有什么规律吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, it's interesting because a lot of them, I wish there was an answer in the back of the book where there was one thing.
zh: 是的，这很有意思，因为其中很多，我真希望书背后有答案，只有一条答案。

speaker: Unknown
en: Maybe one observation, Lenny, is they come from a variety of places.
zh: 也许一个观察，Lenny,是它们来自各种各样的地方。

speaker: Unknown
en: So one lesson I've always felt is you always have to be watching for something that catches your eye.
zh: 所以我一直觉得的一个经验教训是，你总是要留意那些能吸引你眼球的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: Maybe we come back to that in a second.
zh: 也许我们过一会儿再回到这个话题。

speaker: Unknown
en: They very rarely, at least in my experience, have come from design sprints or times where you set aside on a calendar, okay, we're going to go come up with our next idea.
zh: 在我的经验里，它们很少来自设计冲刺，或者你在日历上专门留出的时间：好，我们要去想我们的下一个点子了。

speaker: Unknown
en: They usually come when people are swimming in the hallway, maybe on a weekend, often over a break, a lot of our Labs teams will be hacking and building on stuff and they just can't help themselves and they'll come back or they'll share a video and be like, "Look at this amazing thing."
zh: 它们通常是人们在走廊里闲聊时出现的，也许在周末，经常是在假期里，我们很多 Labs 团队会去折腾和构建一些东西，他们就是忍不住，然后他们会回来，或者会分享一个视频说：“看看这个神奇的东西。”

speaker: Unknown
en: So I think one lesson is always on alert.
zh: 所以我认为一个经验教训是永远保持警觉。

speaker: Unknown
en: Second lesson is they don't come in conventional places.
zh: 第二个经验教训是它们不会来自常规的地方。

speaker: Unknown
en: You can't microwave good ideas.
zh: 你没法用微波炉加热出好点子。

speaker: Unknown
en: And maybe that leads to a third thing I've seen is sometimes it's about less about the idea and who are the interesting people and more importantly, what are their interesting little side projects and passion things and creating the chemistry around that.
zh: 也许这就引出了我见过的第三点：有时候重点不在于点子本身，也不在于谁是那些有意思的人，而更重要的是他们那些有意思的小型副业项目和热爱的事情，并围绕这些营造化学反应。

speaker: Unknown
en: Because usually what we found, at least in Labs over the last four or five years, is that all these ideas, whether they're Notebook or Flow or AI Studio or Google Beam or any of this stuff, they get started by very small groups of people who are just obsessed and usually very curious about something and they just won't stop.
zh: 因为通常我们发现，至少在 Labs 过去的四五年里，所有这些点子，不管是 Notebook 还是 Flow 还是 AI Studio 还是 Google Beam 还是这些东西中的任何一个，都是由非常小的一群人启动的，他们只是对某件事着迷，通常好奇心极强，而且就是停不下来。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so you're like, how do you create a space where that can happen and then be on alert to catch it and try to funnel it forward?
zh: 于是你就要想，怎么创造一个能让这种事发生的空间，然后保持警觉去捕捉它，并尝试把它往前引导？

speaker: Unknown
en: So what I'm hearing here is interestingly not design sprints.
zh: 所以我这里听到的是，有意思的是，不是设计冲刺。

speaker: Unknown
en: I didn't hear brainstorm meetings in there as a place good ideas come from.
zh: 我没听到头脑风暴会议是好点子的来源之一。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah.
zh: 是的。

speaker: Unknown
en: Is there an example maybe because someone listening to this, I'm trying to think about what can they take from this to help them find great ideas, say they're a startup founder or at a big company playing with the latest models.
zh: 有没有例子，也许因为正在听这期节目的某个人，我想让他们能从这里带走些什么来帮助他们找到好点子，比如他们是初创公司创始人，或者在大公司里玩最新的模型。

speaker: Unknown
en: What are some of the conditions that you find most help?
zh: 你发现哪些条件最有帮助？

speaker: Unknown
en: Yes, yes.
zh: 有，有。

speaker: Unknown
en: I mean, one thing we try to do a lot, and I think this would apply in any of those situations, is how do you get yourself to the frontier?
zh: 我是说，我们经常尝试做的一件事，而且我认为这适用于任何那些情况，就是怎么让你自己到达前沿？

speaker: Unknown
en: And that can be both with playing with the models, but also just watching what are the types of experiences that have just become possible where we have a phrase on the team, we talk about what's almost possible and we just have a list actually where we're trying to track those things.
zh: 这既可以是玩这些模型，也可以只是观察哪些类型的体验刚刚变得可能，我们团队有一句口头禅，我们谈论什么是「几乎可能」的，而且我们实际上有一个清单，我们在尝试追踪这些东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: And when one crosses over, it's almost like a phase shift when something goes from solid to gas or liquid to gas or something, you're like, "Ooh, that just became possible.
zh: 当其中一个跨越过去时，就像一种相变，当某样东西从固态变成气态，或从液态变成气态之类的时候，你就会想：“哦，那个刚刚变得可能了。

speaker: Unknown
en: I saw one of these two days ago and I can't stop thinking about it."
zh: 两天前我看到了这样一个东西，我一直忍不住想它。”

speaker: Unknown
en: Are you able to tell us or it's a...
zh: 你能告诉我们吗，还是说这是个……

speaker: Unknown
en: Maybe soon.
zh: 也许很快吧。

speaker: Unknown
en: But if you're at the frontier playing with the models, watching what's happening and you have this list, then when you see something, whether it's on X or wherever, then you're like, "Okay, that just now has become possible."
zh: 但如果你在前沿玩着这些模型，观察正在发生的事情，并且你有这样一份清单，那么当你看到某个东西，不管是在 X 还是哪里，你就会想：“好，那个刚刚变得可能了。”

speaker: Unknown
en: And then we try to think about how do we get a team around that and just go.
zh: 然后我们就尝试思考怎么围绕它组建一个团队，直接开干。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so that may be as you're in startup land, if you're thinking or maybe you're starting to pitch ideas to VCs or whatever, that's kind of how I'd be trying to think about.
zh: 所以这可能就是，当你在创业世界里，如果你在想，或者也许你开始向 VC 们推销点子之类的，那大概就是我尝试思考问题的方式。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then of course, tech alone isn't enough.
zh: 当然，光有技术是不够的。

speaker: Unknown
en: You've got to match that to an interesting user problem.
zh: 你得把它匹配到一个有意思的用户问题上。

speaker: Unknown
en: And ideally, if you can put those together in a way that's so good, people will pay for it.
zh: 而且理想情况下，如果你能把这两者以一种好得不得了的方式结合在一起，人们会愿意付费。

speaker: Unknown
en: That's kind of the combination of things we start looking for pretty early.
zh: 这大概就是我们很早就开始寻找的那些东西的组合。

speaker: Unknown
en: So that's an interesting tactic there is make a list of what is almost possible and then watch for, okay, wow, this is now possible.
zh: 所以这里有个有意思的策略，就是列一份「什么是几乎可能的」清单，然后留意：好，哇，这个现在可能了。

speaker: Unknown
en: Let's explore this now.
zh: 我们现在来探索这个。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, that's right.
zh: 是的，没错。

speaker: Unknown
en: Is there anything on that list you can share of things that are not yet possible but almost possible that you're waiting for or watching for?
zh: 那份清单上有没有什么你可以分享的、那些还不可能但几乎可能、你正在等待或关注的事情?

speaker: Unknown
en: Well, maybe I can share a few areas because I think how we think about it in Labs is we have a bit of a thought experiment we go through where we're like, what is the future of a certain thing going to look like?
zh: 嗯,也许我可以分享几个领域,因为我认为我们在 Labs 里看待这个问题的方式是,我们会做一个思想实验,我们会问,某个东西的未来会是什么样子?

speaker: Unknown
en: So the future of software design and development or the future of creativity, the future of work or knowledge.
zh: 比如软件设计与开发的未来,或者创造力的未来、工作或知识的未来。

speaker: Unknown
en: One area we're watching very close right now is just what is the future of entertainment going to look like?
zh: 我们现在非常密切关注的一个领域就是,娱乐的未来会是什么样子?

speaker: Unknown
en: And this whole idea around immersive entertainment is super interesting just at a technical level for many reasons, but also you think about just the user sort of behaviors and what does entertainment look like last year, this year versus next year, maybe in three years.

speaker: Unknown
en: That's why hundreds of enterprises, including Snowflake, Sony and BNY use the DX platform to measure AI's impact on developer productivity.
zh: 这就是为什么数百家企业，包括 Snowflake、索尼和 BNY，使用 DX 平台来度量 AI 对开发者生产力的影响。

speaker: Unknown
en: Visit getdx.com/lenny to get a demo of DX.
zh: 访问 getdx.com/lenny 获取 DX 的演示。

speaker: Unknown
en: That's getdx.com/lenny.
zh: 网址是 getdx.com/lenny。

speaker: Unknown
en: What skills are you finding are trending up in value in the people that you're working with and what do you feel are trending down when you look at people that are doing really well now?
zh: 你发现和你共事的人当中，哪些技能的价值正在上升，而当你看现在做得非常好的人时，你觉得哪些正在下降？

speaker: Unknown
en: What are the attributes and skills of those people versus things that are maybe less important now?
zh: 这些人的特质和技能是什么，对比那些现在可能没那么重要的东西？

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, I feel like there's a whole lot out there on taste and judgment and vibe coding and all of that.
zh: 是的，我觉得关于品味、判断力和 vibe coding 以及所有这些，外面已经有很多讨论了。

speaker: Unknown
en: I guess the things I'm looking for, I'm always trying to find what are the misprice signals?
zh: 我要找的东西，我一直在试图发现哪些是被错误定价的信号？

speaker: Unknown
en: And so, one I think is we'll hear sometimes people talk about what's someone's learning rate.
zh: 所以，其中一个是我们有时会听到人们谈论一个人的学习率是什么。

speaker: Unknown
en: Do they have a growth mindset?
zh: 他们有没有成长型思维？

speaker: Unknown
en: What's their learning rate?
zh: 他们的学习率是什么？

speaker: Unknown
en: I'm actually looking a lot right now for people, what's their unlearning rate?
zh: 我现在实际上很看重的一点是人们的「遗忘学习率」(unlearning rate)是什么。

speaker: Unknown
en: How fast can they learn something and then walk away from it?
zh: 他们能多快学会一样东西,然后又把它放下?

speaker: Unknown
en: Based on maybe what they're seeing when they test their product or something.
zh: 依据可能是他们在测试自己的产品时看到的东西之类的。

speaker: Unknown
en: So unlearning rate is one.
zh: 所以「遗忘学习率」是一个。

speaker: Unknown
en: Another one I'm interested in, I read a book a year or so ago about Roger Federer, the amazing tennis player.
zh: 另一个我感兴趣的,我大约一年前读过一本关于 Roger Federer 那位了不起的网球运动员的书。

speaker: Unknown
en: And there was this phrase in there about Federer had explosive endurance.
zh: 书里有一句话,说 Federer 拥有「爆发性耐力」(explosive endurance)。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's just this beautiful turn of phrase and with the alliteration and everything, but it's like there's something around how are people taking care of themselves and the people around them where they can go really hard and that's the explosive part, but they can do it over a while and they find ways to pace themselves.
zh: 这是一个很美的措辞,还有头韵什么的,意思大概是:人们如何照顾好自己和身边的人,使他们能够全力冲刺——这是「爆发」的部分——但又能持续很长一段时间,并找到为自己调节节奏的方法。

speaker: Unknown
en: In Labs, we have seasons of Labs where we talk about this.
zh: 在 Labs,我们有一些关于这个话题的「Labs 季节」(seasons of Labs),我们会谈论这个。

speaker: Unknown
en: So I think that explosive endurance, this unlearning rate.
zh: 所以我认为「爆发性耐力」,以及这个「遗忘学习率」。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then maybe another one I would say is as much as coding and other things are becoming maybe trending towards you being able to direct lots of agents and not having to work with as many people, I still feel like collaboration and how you work with people matters even more now.
zh: 然后我想再说的另一个是,尽管编程和其他事情正趋向于你能够指挥大量智能体、不必和那么多人一起工作,我仍然觉得协作以及你与人合作的方式现在甚至更重要了。

speaker: Unknown
en: And one of the things we look a lot for is can someone blend and bridge these worlds where they're incredible collaborator with an agent or a swarm of agents, but also with people?
zh: 我们非常看重的一点是:一个人能否融合并 bridging 这两个世界——既能与一个智能体或一群智能体成为出色的协作者,也能与人协作?

speaker: Unknown
en: And I guess what we believe on the Labs team and on the Gemini team is that there's still just so much joy in working with people.
zh: 我想我们在 Labs 团队和 Gemini 团队上的信念是,与人一起工作仍然有太多的乐趣。

speaker: Unknown
en: But it's like how do you find the right chemistry?
zh: 但问题是你如何找到合适的化学反应?

speaker: Unknown
en: And so maybe one thing I'd say there is people that can build trust, that can scale trust, that underpins any kind of great collaboration.
zh: 所以也许我想说的是那些能够建立信任、能够扩展信任的人,这是一切伟大协作的基础。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so that's another maybe signal I'm always looking for is how fast can this person build trust with people and create that kind of environment, if that makes sense.
zh: 所以这是我一直寻找的另一个信号:这个人能多快与人建立信任,并创造出那种环境——如果我表达得清楚的话。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, these are so interesting.
zh: 是的,这些非常有意思。

speaker: Unknown
en: On that last one, is that kind of a growing, emerging, even more important skill you're finding with the rise of AI?
zh: 关于最后那一点,随着 AI 的兴起,你是否发现这是一种正在增长、新兴、甚至更重要的技能?

speaker: Unknown
en: And I'm curious why.
zh: 我很好奇为什么。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think so for a couple of reasons.
zh: 我认为是的,有几个原因。

speaker: Unknown
en: I would say one maybe is uniquely Google.
zh: 我想其中一个可能是 Google 独有的。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's a larger organization, so you've got to be able to do that.
zh: 这是一个更大的组织,所以你必须能够做到这一点。

speaker: Unknown
en: But the ones that don't feel uniquely Google, one, it feels like as the execution costs of making products goes down, we'll be able to make more products, which you may make the same products with the same people, but I think there's a lot more, you probably see this too, is just people will team up with different people to make stuff.
zh: 但那些感觉不是 Google 独有的原因,其一,随着做产品的执行成本下降,我们将能够做出更多产品,你可能用同样的人做同样的产品,但我认为还有更多的——你可能也看到了——就是人们会和不同的人组队来做东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so it's very interesting when we're thinking about almost like fielding a new team for a Labs project where you used to say it's about five to seven people.
zh: 所以这很有意思,当我们考虑为 Labs 项目几乎像组建一支新队伍时,你过去会说大概是五到七个人。

speaker: Unknown
en: Now it's about two to three people, maybe four.
zh: 现在大概是两到三个人,也许四个。

speaker: Unknown
en: But it's kind of like those people just almost... You can almost imagine super talented musicians who team up with different people and then they play different songs together, the songs are the products.
zh: 但这有点像这些人几乎……你几乎可以想象那些超级有才华的音乐家,他们与不同的人组队,然后一起演奏不同的歌曲,歌曲就是产品。

speaker: Unknown
en: But it's like those are the MVPs in Labs where you can be like, "Hey, drop this sort of PM," but that can also code and design because all the roles are blurring with other people and see how they jam on stuff together.
zh: 但这就像是 Labs 里的那些 MVP,你可以说:「嘿,换掉这个 PM」,但那个人同时也能写代码和做设计,因为所有的角色都在与他人互相模糊,然后看他们如何即兴合作。

speaker: Unknown
en: So I think that's where my prediction is that skill will almost increase in importance because there will be more products and because there'll be more of this free agents kind of jamming on stuff together.
zh: 所以我的预测是,这项技能的重要性几乎会增加,因为会有更多的产品,而且会有更多这种自由智能体(free agents)一起即兴合作做东西的情况。

speaker: Unknown
en: Along those lines, I imagine you have been pulling designers, engineers, NPMs into Labs and they all work together and sometimes different functions take leads.
zh: 沿着这个思路,我想你一直在把设计师、工程师、NPM 拉进 Labs,他们都一起工作,有时不同职能会轮流主导。

speaker: Unknown
en: Has there been a shift in who you find is most impactful and successful in leading product ideas, Labs, teams in terms of the ratio of PM versus design versus eng?
zh: 在主导产品创意、Labs、团队方面,就 PM 相对于设计相对于工程的比例而言,你是否发现最有影响力和最成功的人选发生了变化?

speaker: Unknown
en: For example, are PMs becoming more valuable or eng becoming more valuable, something like that?
zh: 比如,PM 正变得更有价值,还是工程师正变得更有价值,之类的?

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, it's interesting.
zh: 是的,这很有意思。

speaker: Unknown
en: We've been studying this a lot and actually testing a lot of this too.
zh: 我们一直在大量研究这个,实际上也做了很多测试。

speaker: Unknown
en: I would say in general, PM happens to be the function maybe by nature because it's a bit more horizontal, that feels like it's maybe being able to adapt to some of the other functions faster.
zh: 我想说,总体而言,PM 这个职能——也许由于它的本质,因为它更横向一些——感觉它也许能更快地适应其他一些职能。

speaker: Unknown
en: And we see this when we'll run little builder pilots across the company that comes back as like, oh yeah, that's maybe, I don't want to say it's easier, but maybe it's PMs are more accustomed to like, all right, I'm in this meeting, I got to simulate something as a lawyer or as a BD person or as a sales... Do you know what I mean?
zh: 我们在公司内部运行小型 builder 试点时会看到这一点,反馈回来的结果是:哦对,那也许……我不想说它更容易,但也许是 PM 更习惯于:好吧,我在这场会议里,我得扮演一个律师、一个 BD 的人或一个销售来做模拟……你懂我的意思吗?

speaker: Unknown
en: So I think in some way maybe there's some inherentness in who selects into that.
zh: 所以我认为在某种程度上,选择进入这个职能的人本身也许有某种内在特质。

speaker: Unknown
en: So that definitely is true.
zh: 所以这肯定是对的。

speaker: Unknown
en: But I would say our best people can come from any function.
zh: 但我想说,我们最优秀的人可以来自任何职能。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I would also even widen it, Lenny, we're seeing strategy and ops people and PD people and marketing people be builders in Labs and they are really good.
zh: 我甚至想把它扩大,Lenny,我们看到战略和运营的人、PD 的人、市场的人都在 Labs 里做 builder,而且他们非常出色。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think maybe this is another overhyped, underhyped thing.
zh: 我想这也许是另一个「被高估/被低估」的话题。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think right now people are maybe overhyping like everybody's a builder and it's just this new job function and everything's kind of the same.
zh: 我觉得现在人们也许在过度炒作「人人都是 builder」,好像这只是一个新的职能,一切都差不多一样。

speaker: Unknown
en: I actually feel like at least what we're seeing is that people still have their specialty.
zh: 我实际的感觉是,至少我们观察到的是,人们仍然保有他们的专长。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's like their major or minor in college or something.
zh: 就像是他们大学里的专业或辅修之类的。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I feel like there's a risk if everybody becomes a builder that you lose a lot of respect and appreciation and obviously the expertise that comes from those specialties.
zh: 而我觉得存在一个风险:如果人人都变成 builder,你会失去很多来自那些专长的尊重、欣赏,以及显而易见的专业知识。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so I think when we set up teams, even though we may be like, this is more of a builder crew, we're still thinking about where are the specialties?
zh: 所以我认为当我们组建团队时,即使我们可能会说「这更像是一支 builder 队伍」,我们仍然在考虑专长在哪里?

speaker: Unknown
en: And that ends up being super important as well.
zh: 而这最终也变得超级重要。

speaker: Unknown
en: I completely agree.
zh: 我完全同意。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, I like that.
zh: 是的,我喜欢这个。

speaker: Unknown
en: I like this metaphor of the major and minor.
zh: 我喜欢这个主修和辅修的比喻。

speaker: Unknown
en: That's a really fun way to think about it.
zh: 这是一个思考这件事非常有趣的方式。

speaker: Unknown
en: You can be better at building, but your PM skills are still the primary thing you're amazing at.
zh: 你可以在 building 方面变得更强,但你的 PM 技能仍然是你最擅长的主业。

speaker: Unknown
en: Definitely.
zh: 当然。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think that's the advice we give, especially to a lot of new PMs on the teams, like APMs or people earlier in their career is it's great you're vibe coding and you're making all these prototypes, but do that in service of becoming an exceptional, extraordinary PM and don't lose that major.
zh: 我认为这就是我们给的建议，尤其是给团队里很多新 PM,比如 APM 或者职业早期的人，就是你在 vibe coding、在做这些原型，这很棒，但要以此服务于成为一个卓越的、非凡的 PM,不要丢了主线。

speaker: Unknown
en: That's what you need to hone, especially when you're early on.
zh: 那才是你需要磨练的，尤其是在早期的时候。

speaker: Unknown
en: I love the way you described it where PMs are really good at simulating other functions, such an AI way of thinking about collaborating.
zh: 我很喜欢你描述它的方式，PM 真的很擅长模拟其他职能，这是一种 AI 式的协作思考方式。

speaker: Unknown
en: And this idea of explosive endurance, someone tweeted this recently.
zh: 还有这个“爆发性耐力”的概念，最近有人在推特上提到这个。

speaker: Unknown
en: They're like, "What's so called when it's both a marathon and a sprint?"
zh: 他们说，“既是马拉松又是冲刺，这叫什么？”

speaker: Unknown
en: It's that.
zh: 就是那个。

speaker: Unknown
en: It was like, "Talk to Roger Federer."
zh: 那条像是“去问 Roger Federer。”

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah.
zh: 是啊。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah.
zh: 是啊。

speaker: Unknown
en: I feel like everyone's in that right now.
zh: 我感觉现在每个人都处于那种状态。

speaker: Unknown
en: And that's just a constant theme and trend on this podcast and just in tech right now is just everyone's in this marathon plus sprint mode.
zh: 这也是这个播客上、也是现在科技圈一直反复出现的主题和趋势，就是每个人都处于这种马拉松加冲刺的模式。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yes.
zh: 是的。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah.
zh: 是啊。

speaker: Unknown
en: Man, I guess is there anything that you do to help people deal with that because it feels like it's nonstop?
zh: 天哪，我想问，你有没有做什么来帮助大家应对这种状态？因为感觉这永无止境。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah.
zh: 有。

speaker: Unknown
en: I mean, one of the things we try to do, I mentioned a little bit earlier, but I can unpack it some, is we think of seasons in Labs and can we think about at any given point there's 20 or 30 experiment running simultaneously, but for each individual little team trying to create a little bit of milestones or a rhythm to the work.
zh: 我的意思是，我们尝试做的事情之一，我之前稍微提到过，但我可以展开讲讲，就是我们在 Labs 里以“赛季”来思考，我们能不能做到在任何时间点都有二三十个实验同时进行，但让每个小团队都尝试为工作创造一些里程碑或节奏。

speaker: Unknown
en: And there's sometimes it is just flat out full on.
zh: 而有时候确实就是彻头彻尾的全速推进。

speaker: Unknown
en: And maybe the best lesson I've learned as a leader is almost to sort of name that, declare that people opt in or opt out of that, but also be very clear when a team is not in that mode.
zh: 也许我作为领导者学到的最好的一课，就是几乎要把这一点点明、宣告出来，让人们选择加入或退出这种状态，同时也要非常清楚什么时候团队不处于那种模式。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think it's like how do you try to architect almost like a rhythm to the year where it's like, "Hey, we've got a big model coming.
zh: 我认为这就像是，你怎么去设计一种几乎是一年之中的节奏，比如“嘿，我们有一个大模型要来了。

speaker: Unknown
en: These five products are super important to showcase this model.
zh: 这五款产品对展示这个模型超级重要。

speaker: Unknown
en: We think this model will propel them."
zh: 我们认为这个模型会推动它们。”

speaker: Unknown
en: You five is like, "It is explosive time."
zh: 你们五个，就是“现在是爆发时刻。”

speaker: Unknown
en: Do you know what I mean?
zh: 你懂我的意思吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: And so it's trying to create a common language around that, which is sometimes in a lot of ways PMs sometimes can be very effective if they can come up with what is the sort of shorthand or the common language.
zh: 所以就是尝试围绕这一点创造一种共同语言，这在很多方面，如果 PM 能想出什么是 shorthand 或者共同语言，他们有时会非常高效。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so we actually put a lot of thought into that too of like, "All right, you all are on right now."
zh: 所以我们实际上也在这方面投入了很多思考，比如“好，你们现在上场。”

speaker: Unknown
en: Whereas after they go through that, we may be say after a Google IO, a lot of Labs teams will sprint.
zh: 而在他们经历那之后，我们可能会说，比如在 Google IO 之后，很多 Labs 团队会冲刺。

speaker: Unknown
en: After IO, June is like, "Hey, just go hack, go rediscover what's new, just go build, have fun."
zh: IO 之后的六月就像，“嘿，去 hack 吧，去重新发现有什么新东西，就去构建，玩得开心。”

speaker: Unknown
en: And then it's so interesting, Lenny, because the instinct or the temptation is like, "Oh, man, it's June.
zh: 然后这很有意思，Lenny,因为直觉或诱惑是，“哦，天哪，现在是六月。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's unproductive.
zh: 没有产出。

speaker: Unknown
en: We're not shipping."
zh: 我们没有在发布东西。”

speaker: Unknown
en: And it's like, no, actually those are where all the new seeds are coming from for the next season.
zh: 但其实不是，实际上那正是下一个赛季所有新种子的来源。

speaker: Unknown
en: Do you know what I mean?
zh: 你懂我的意思吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: And so it's trying to think through the rhythm of that is one way we try to do it.
zh: 所以尝试想清楚这个节奏，是我们尝试做到这一点的一种方式。

speaker: Unknown
en: I don't think we always get it right though, by the way.
zh: 不过顺便说一下，我不认为我们总是能做对。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think one of the things we're talking a lot on the team is, I guess in the past, people would talk about work-life balance and there were other ways this conversation got framed.
zh: 而且我认为我们在团队里经常讨论的一件事是，我想过去人们会谈论工作与生活的平衡，这场对话还有其他的框架。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think why I like things like explosive endurance or concepts like that is we want to be doing this as a team for many, many years.
zh: 我认为我为什么喜欢“爆发性耐力”或类似概念，是因为我们想作为一个团队做这件事很多很多年。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so it's like you can't just empty the tank in nine months and just kill yourself.
zh: 所以你不能在九个月内就把油箱清空、把自己累垮。

speaker: Unknown
en: So you have to have a view towards the long term, but also recognize the moment you're in is fast.
zh: 所以你必须有面向长期的视角，但也要认识到你所处的时刻是很快的。

speaker: Unknown
en: I love the tactic of just naming it, having a lot of power and just making it clear this is the mode we're in now and won't be forever.
zh: 我很喜欢“点明它”这个策略，这很有力量，就是清楚地表明：这是我们现在所处的模式，而且不会永远如此。

speaker: Unknown
en: Right, right.
zh: 对，对。

speaker: Unknown
en: And something I've found is the opposite also is dangerous when you have too little to do and too little stress and too little pedal on the metal.
zh: 而且我发现反过来的情况同样危险，就是当你事情太少、压力太小、踩油门太轻的时候。

speaker: Unknown
en: People get bored and start looking for other jobs.
zh: 人们会感到无聊，开始找其他工作。

speaker: Unknown
en: They're just like, "This sucks."
zh: 他们会说，“这太糟糕了。”

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, yeah.
zh: 是啊，是啊。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah.
zh: 是的。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think there's always something there though, you're right, of we talk on the team a little bit of never waste an event or a date or you can think about even as a startup, where's that moment you want to intersect with something in the world?
zh: 不过我认为总有可以做的，你说得对，我们在团队里会有点谈论“绝不浪费一个活动或一个日期”，你甚至可以以创业公司的角度来思考，你想与世界上某个事物相交的那个时刻在哪里？

speaker: Unknown
en: And whether that for us is a Google IO or a model release or whatever, I think that's always healthy to be thinking about.
zh: 不管对我们来说是 Google IO 还是一次模型发布还是别的什么，我认为思考这个总是健康的。

speaker: Unknown
en: I got a question the other day on Gemini.
zh: 前几天我收到一个关于 Gemini 的问题。

speaker: Unknown
en: They were like, "What's our two-year roadmap?"
zh: 他们问，“我们的两年路线图是什么？”

speaker: Unknown
en: And I was like, "We have a six-month roadmap on this team."
zh: 我当时就说：“我们这个团队有一个六个月的路线图。”

speaker: Unknown
en: We have a multi-year vision, but I think the world has changed so much too.
zh: 我们有一个多年的愿景，但我觉得这个世界也变化得太快了。

speaker: Unknown
en: Some of it is like the thing I saw two days ago is now a project that happened in 48 hours.
zh: 有点像我两天前看到的东西，现在变成了一个 48 小时内就做出来的项目。

speaker: Unknown
en: You can't plan for that in a way.
zh: 你在某种程度上没法为此做规划。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so that's the other element you almost have to recognize in the moment.
zh: 所以这是另一个要素，你几乎必须在当下就意识到。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah.
zh: 是啊。

speaker: Unknown
en: So along those lines, how has planning changed in the past couple years?
zh: 那么，沿着这个思路，过去几年规划发生了什么变化？

speaker: Unknown
en: You guys are different from the rest of Google because everything is new, but just what have you seen in terms of timelines and timeframes shift in planning with the rise of AI?
zh: 所以你大致能掌握模型整体的节奏。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, we usually are thinking somewhere on the order of about six months.
zh: 是的，我们通常考虑的时间尺度大约是六个月左右。

speaker: Unknown
en: And usually I say that because that's that almost possible window where you assume every lab is cranking out some new pre-training model a couple times a year.
zh: 我这么说是因为这几乎是一个可能的窗口期，你假设每个实验室每年都会推出几次新的预训练模型。

speaker: Unknown
en: There's individual points in between.
zh: 中间还有一些个别的节点。

speaker: Unknown
en: So you kind of have an overall cadence of where the models are.
zh: 所以你对模型的整体节奏大概有一个把握。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then I think we are almost imagining in about a hundred days usually, we always think about where can you move your product meaningfully forward?
zh: 然后我觉得我们几乎总是在设想大约一百天的时间，我们总在想，你能在哪里让产品有实质性的前进？

speaker: Unknown
en: Our best Labs team, they all do that.
zh: 我们最好的 Labs 团队，他们都是这么做的。

speaker: Unknown
en: They'll go from idea to some meaningful milestone in 50 to 100 days.
zh: 他们会在 50 到 100 天内从一个想法做到某个有意义的里程碑。

speaker: Unknown
en: And part of that is also how do you design a culture and an environment where you unblock a lot of stuff so you can just let people cook?
zh: 其中一部分也是你如何设计一种文化和环境，让你解除很多东西的阻塞，这样你就可以让人们放手去干？

speaker: Unknown
en: And so that's the other part of is creating that environment.
zh: 所以这是另一部分，就是创造那样的环境。

speaker: Unknown
en: But we think about planning as kind of almost like rolling six months maybe to answer your question.
zh: 不过要回答你的问题，我们把规划看作几乎是一种滚动式的六个月。

speaker: Unknown
en: So I had this Lenny and Friends summit, it was last week of the day we're recording this, and Dan Shipper gave this really interesting talk about how to build where the tech is just constantly changing underneath you.
zh: 我办了一个 Lenny and Friends 峰会，就录这期节目的那一周，Dan Shipper 做了一个非常有趣的演讲，讲的是当技术在你的脚下不断变化时，如何构建。

speaker: Unknown
en: And his advice is to have a frontier team that's dedicated to testing out the new stuff.
zh: 他的建议是成立一个专门负责测试新东西的前沿团队。

speaker: Unknown
en: And basically it's their job, try all the new stuff, report on what we need to pay attention to so that the rest of the company can not have to be distracted and focus on the task at hand.
zh: 基本上这就是他们的工作，尝试所有新东西，报告我们需要关注什么，这样公司其他人就不必分心，可以专注于手头的任务。

speaker: Unknown
en: How do you feel about that as a model for companies?
zh: 你觉得这作为一种公司模式怎么样？

speaker: Unknown
en: I think every company definitely needs a set of people, a team, however you want to manifest it.
zh: 我认为每家公司肯定都需要一群人、一个团队，不管你想以什么形式体现。

speaker: Unknown
en: That is, their job is to be at the frontier and they're almost like if they haven't heard about the latest hot thing viral on X in the last 24 hours is like, what are you doing at your job?
zh: 也就是说，他们的工作就是站在前沿，如果他们在过去 24 小时内没听说过 X 上最新爆火的东西，就好像在问：你上班都在干什么？

speaker: Unknown
en: So I think there's definitely an element of you want people plugged in to the hive mind of how people are building and thinking and all the model releases.
zh: 所以我认为你肯定需要让人们接入那个集体思维，了解人们如何构建、如何思考，以及所有的模型发布。

speaker: Unknown
en: They're the people who have eight, $200 a month subscriptions on everything.
zh: 他们就是那种在所有平台上都有八个月费 200 美元订阅的人。

speaker: Unknown
en: Do you know what I mean?
zh: 你懂我的意思吧？

speaker: Unknown
en: So you have to architect the organization where that can exist.
zh: 所以你必须设计好组织架构，让这种角色能够存在。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think the second thing though that's just as important is the environment of which those people can build.
zh: 不过我认为第二件同样重要的事，是这些人可以进行构建的环境。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so that's the other maybe part of that.
zh: 所以那可能是另一部分。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then I think the third part, which is honestly where if you look at the history, and I've read a bunch of books on this because most, if you just look at the data, a large company who starts a lab, the lab is usually ineffective and fizzles out after about three to four years.
zh: 然后我认为第三部分，老实说，如果你看历史，我也读过不少这方面的书，因为大多数，如果只看数据的话，一家大公司创办一个实验室，这个实验室通常收效甚微，大约三四年后就不了了之。

speaker: Unknown
en: Or it may have duration, but the company can never commercialize the things coming out of the lab.
zh: 或者它可能存续下来，但公司永远无法把实验室产出的东西商业化。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so you get things like someone comes by and sees the future and then they do it as a separate company or whatever.
zh: 于是就会出现这种情况：有人过来看到了未来，然后他们作为一家独立的公司去做，或者诸如此类。

speaker: Unknown
en: And there's famous examples throughout history of that.
zh: 历史上有很多这样著名的例子。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so I think there is this interesting balance of can you have a team of people who live at the frontier like Dan says, who are building frontier things but can somehow bridge or connect across the bigger company in a way that it's not, oh, that's just some weird R&D group always coming up with gimmicks and toys?
zh: 所以我认为有一种有趣的平衡：你能不能拥有一群像 Dan 说的那样活在前沿的人，他们在构建前沿的东西，但又能以某种方式跨越或连接到更大的公司，而不是让人觉得，哦，那只是一个总在搞噱头和玩具的奇怪研发小组？

speaker: Unknown
en: Do you know what I mean?
zh: 你懂我的意思吧？

speaker: Unknown
en: And so I think it takes a certain person or a certain set of people who can actually be like, "Hey, that thing looks like a toy right now.
zh: 所以我认为这需要某一种人或者某一群人，他们真的能够说出：“嘿，那东西现在看起来像个玩具。

speaker: Unknown
en: That's going to be essential to our future in five years."
zh: 但五年后它将对我们的未来至关重要。”

speaker: Unknown
en: And that's actually where, at least studying history, where sometimes these frontier ideas fall short, you can get the first two things right and then fail on the third one and then the whole thing really doesn't matter.
zh: 而实际上，至少从研究历史来看，这正是这些前沿想法有时失败的地方，你可以把前两件事做对，然后在第三件事上失败，然后整个事情就真的不重要了。

speaker: Unknown
en: Do you know what I mean?
zh: 你懂我的意思吧？

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah.
zh: 是啊。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's interesting as just even Anthropic has a labs team, the most cutting edge company, they're just at the frontier already.
zh: 有意思的是，就连 Anthropic 也有一个 labs 团队，作为最尖端的公司，他们本身就已经在前沿了。

speaker: Unknown
en: They're like, "Okay, but we also need a labs team to actually watch the frontier frontier."
zh: 他们说：“好吧，但我们还需要一个 labs 团队来真正盯着那个前沿的前沿。”

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, that's right.
zh: 是的，没错。

speaker: Unknown
en: Well, one thing we joke about too inside as Labs has grown now and we've had a few projects thankfully have kind of hit and are lots of users now and growing, we've actually internally to this point of common language, what we started to find was a bigger project like Notebook in terms of users or Flow or AI Studio or these things that are grown out of Labs.
zh: 嗯，我们内部还开的一个玩笑是，随着 Labs 现在的成长，谢天谢地我们已经有几个项目算是打出来了，现在有很多用户而且还在增长，实际上对应刚才说的共同语言这一点，我们开始发现一个更大的项目，比如用户规模方面的 Notebook，或者 Flow、AI Studio，或者这些从 Labs 生长出来的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: In some ways there's a risk they crowd out the zero to one stuff.
zh: 某种程度上，存在它们挤占从零到一项目的风险。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so the terms we've started using is there's zero to one Labs, there's one to 10 Labs, and there's 10 to 100.
zh: 所以我们开始使用的术语是：有从零到一的 Labs，有一到十的 Labs，还有十到一百的。

speaker: Unknown
en: And these may not mean anything to your audience, but to us, we actually have kind of encoded these are different stages of the Labs life cycle and we want all of these products to have this innovative energy that's common, but inside each of those stages, there's very different challenges and very different things you're optimizing for.
zh: 这些可能对你的听众没什么意义，但对我们来说，我们实际上已经把这些编码成了 Labs 生命周期的不同阶段，我们希望所有这些产品都有那种共同的创新能量，但在每个阶段内部，面临的挑战非常不同，你优化的东西也非常不同。

speaker: Unknown
en: And in zero to one, you're looking at eyeballs like we talked about.
zh: 在从零到一，你看的是眼球数，就像我们谈过的。

speaker: Unknown
en: And in maybe 10 to 100, you're looking at waterfalls and CPAs and thinking about how are we actually converting people to these magic moments in the product?
zh: 而在大概十到一百，你看的是瀑布流和 CPA，思考我们如何真正把用户转化到产品里的那些魔法时刻？

speaker: Unknown
en: And it's a scaling game in a lot of way.
zh: 在很多方面来说，这是一个规模化的游戏。

speaker: Unknown
en: Say someone listening is convinced they should set up a frontier team, a Labs team, and it feels like Labs teams have evolved a little bit and it used to be build the next big business unit is the idea here.
zh: 假设某个听众已经确信他们应该建立一个前沿团队，一个 Labs 团队，而且感觉 Labs 团队已经演变了一些，以前的理念是打造下一个大型业务部门。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's like, okay, what's a new technology that is unlocking something or a core business?
zh: 就像是，好吧，有什么新技术正在解锁某个核心业务？

speaker: Unknown
en: I wonder if that's true, but that's what it feels like to me.
zh: 我不确定这是否属实，但这是我个人的感觉。

speaker: Unknown
en: But I guess just with that in mind, what are maybe three tips for someone that wants to set up a Labs team internally?
zh: 但我想带着这个想法，对于一个想在内部建立 Labs 团队的人，有没有三条建议？

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah.
zh: 是的。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think one, you've got to try to create a space where weird things can grow and you can't just nestle this under an existing business unit.
zh: 我认为第一，你必须尽力创造一个让奇怪的东西可以生长的空间，你不能只是把这个塞进现有的业务部门底下。

speaker: Unknown
en: It has to have its own kind of independence is one.
zh: 它必须拥有自己的某种独立性，这是第一点。

speaker: Unknown
en: And in some companies that means it needs to report to the CEO or it needs to report into enough of a distance in a way.
zh: 在某些公司，这意味着它需要直接向 CEO 汇报，或者说它需要在一定程度上保持足够的距离。

speaker: Unknown
en: And we can go into that if you want, but that's super important.
zh: 如果你愿意我们可以深入聊这个，但这超级重要。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think the second thing is a set of people, and in the case of us, this was this user's first, Google second, Labs third thinking where the job of the lab is to make users successful and make Google successful.
zh: 我认为第二件事是一组人，就我们的情况而言，这是「用户第一，Google 第二，Labs 第三」的思维方式，实验室的职责是让用户成功，让 Google 成功。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's not to make itself successful.
zh: 而不是让它自己成功。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so there's a bit of maybe a humility or a collaboration or this mindset of what does success look like?
zh: 所以这里面有一点也许是谦逊，或者协作，或者这种「成功是什么样子」的心态。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think for us, how we've broken that down and how I would encourage companies to think about it is your goal of this labs to graduate things to existing products or is your goal to go invent new product lines and categories?
zh: 而我认为对于我们来说，我们如何拆解这个问题，以及我会如何鼓励公司去思考的是：你这个实验室的目标是把东西「毕业」到现有产品中去，还是你的目标是去发明全新的产品线和品类？

speaker: Unknown
en: And in our case, we started and it was a graduation lab and it's expanded over time as we've started to realize AI really transforms and blurs a lot of categories.
zh: 在我们的案例中，我们起步时是一个「毕业型」实验室，随着我们开始意识到 AI 真的在转变并模糊很多品类，它随着时间扩展了。

speaker: Unknown
en: But being very clear about what game you're playing and what does winning or losing look like would be the second thing.
zh: 但非常清楚你在玩的是什么游戏，赢或输是什么样子，这是第二件事。

speaker: Unknown
en: So isolated in some way, but also part of the same team.
zh: 所以在某种程度上是隔离的，但同时也是同一个团队的一部分。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think the third thing, and we talk about this a little bit on Labs is, and I can imagine for maybe CEOs listening or other kind of C-suite people, use your lab not just for product development or technology exploration, but even for challenging how the company works and almost the way things happen.
zh: 而我认为第三件事，我们在 Labs 里也稍微谈到过这个，而且我可以想象对于可能在听的 CEO 或其他 C 级高管来说，把你的实验室不仅用于产品开发或技术探索，甚至用于挑战公司的运作方式，几乎是事情发生的方式。

speaker: Unknown
en: And that's actually the phrase we use on the team is Labs sometimes creates good trouble at Google.
zh: 这其实是我们在团队里用的说法，就是 Labs 有时会在 Google 制造「好的麻烦」。

speaker: Unknown
en: So there's bad trouble you don't want to create, but good trouble, give you an example.
zh: 所以有你不想制造的坏麻烦，但好的麻烦，举个例子。

speaker: Unknown
en: We were one of the first teams that were like, we're seeing the job roles blur.
zh: 我们是最早提出「我们看到职位角色正在模糊」的团队之一。

speaker: Unknown
en: We have to have a builder job ladder and we need to think about it differently and we should use Labs as the place to pilot it before we roll it out across Google.
zh: 我们必须有一个 builder 职业晋升通道，我们需要用不同的方式来思考它，我们应该把 Labs 作为试点的地方，然后再推广到整个 Google。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so that's another way you can think of the multidimensionality of a lab in a way.
zh: 所以这是你可以思考实验室多维性的另一种方式。

speaker: Unknown
en: You just think about the processes and ways of working, not just products necessarily.
zh: 你不只是思考产品本身，还要思考流程和工作方式。

speaker: Unknown
en: That's really interesting.
zh: 这真的很有意思。

speaker: Josh Woodward
en: Yeah. Yeah.
zh: 是的。是的。

speaker: Unknown
en: What about the type of people that you would put on this lab team?
zh: 那你会把什么类型的人放到这个实验室团队里？

speaker: Unknown
en: You mentioned this unlearning rate is a really interesting way to think about.
zh: 你提到的这个「遗忘率」是一个很有意思的思考角度。

speaker: Unknown
en: What do you look for and what's a person you want to avoid on the lab team?
zh: 你寻找的是什么，你想在实验室团队里避开的是什么样的人？

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, yeah.
zh: 是的，是的。

speaker: Unknown
en: Great one.
zh: 好问题。

speaker: Unknown
en: Man, we are obsessed about finding people who just can't stop themselves from building.
zh: 天哪，我们痴迷于寻找那些就是停不下来、忍不住要构建的人。

speaker: Unknown
en: I mentioned that earlier.
zh: 我之前提到过这一点。

speaker: Unknown
en: We have a whole doc on the team, Labs in a nutshell.
zh: 我们在团队里有一份完整的文档，叫《Labs 概要》。

speaker: Unknown
en: We have one on Gemini too, Gemini in a nutshell.
zh: 我们也有一份 Gemini 的，《Gemini 概要》。

speaker: Unknown
en: The first week someone joins the team, I email it to them.
zh: 有人加入团队的第一周，我就把它用邮件发给他们。

speaker: Unknown
en: And most of them have seen it before as part of some of our hiring screening too.
zh: 而且他们中的大多数人在我们部分招聘筛选环节就已经看过了。

speaker: Unknown
en: They build all the time.
zh: 他们一直在构建。

speaker: Unknown
en: They're intellectually curious.
zh: 他们有求知欲。

speaker: Unknown
en: They're reading, they're on X, they're listening to podcasts.
zh: 他们在阅读，他们在刷 X，他们在听播客。

speaker: Unknown
en: They are obsessed about solving people's problems, not about their own ego or glory.
zh: 他们痴迷于解决别人的问题，而不是自己的自尊或荣耀。

speaker: Unknown
en: They are the people when you're around them, they add energy.
zh: 他们是这样的人，当你和他们在一起时，他们会给你增添能量。

speaker: Unknown
en: You leave a conversation, you're like, "I want to be with that person.
zh: 你结束一段对话后会想，「我想和那个人在一起。

speaker: Unknown
en: I'll run through a wall with that person."
zh: 我愿意和那个人一起翻越一堵墙。」

speaker: Unknown
en: Do you know what I mean?
zh: 你懂我的意思吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: We've got 17 or 18 of them.
zh: 我们有 17 或 18 个这样的人。

speaker: Unknown
en: Maybe I can send some of them to you after if you want to include in the show notes.
zh: 也许之后我可以把其中一些发给你，如果你想放进节目注释里。

speaker: Lenny
en: I'd love that.
zh: 我很乐意。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, but it's such an important part.
zh: 是的，但这是非常重要的一部分。

speaker: Unknown
en: And that third thing I talked about as a tip for setting up a lab, it's not just about job ladders and stuff.
zh: 还有我说的作为建立实验室建议的第三件事，它不只是关于职业晋升通道之类的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's literally about who are the people of the future that you are trying to bring in that are going to think different and challenge things different.
zh: 这其实就是关于你想要吸引的未来的人才是谁,他们会以不同的方式思考,以不同的方式挑战事物。

speaker: Unknown
en: And it's a different type.
zh: 而且这是一种不同的类型。

speaker: Unknown
en: And what we've also found is these products have grown, the zero to one people are different a little bit than the one to 10 and the 10 to 100 too.
zh: 我们还发现,随着这些产品的成长,从零到一的人和从一到十以及从十到一百的人也有些不同。

speaker: Unknown
en: So it's like, how do you create some commonality?
zh: 所以就是,你怎么创造一些共性?

speaker: Unknown
en: But I do think when you're talking to someone, you're looking at...
zh: 但我确实认为,当你和某人交谈时,你是在看……

speaker: Unknown
en: In an interview, if I'm talking to someone, they're like, "Hey, let me show you this thing I just built."
zh: 在面试中,如果我和某人交谈,他们说:“嘿,让我给你看看我刚做的这个东西。”

speaker: Unknown
en: Instant credibility.
zh: 立刻就有了可信度。

speaker: Unknown
en: Or if they're like...
zh: 或者如果他们……

speaker: Unknown
en: I'll ask them questions about unknown, unstructured, dark caves, these events where they don't know which ways forward, how do they figure it out?
zh: 我会问他们关于未知的、无结构的、黑暗洞穴的问题,这些他们不知道哪条路能走通的情境,他们是怎么弄明白的?

speaker: Unknown
en: People that are energized by that huge credibility boost.
zh: 被这种事情激发能量的人,可信度会大大提升。

speaker: Unknown
en: So yeah, there's definitely a certain type that you're looking for.
zh: 所以是的,你寻找的确实是某种特定类型的人。

speaker: Unknown
en: In terms of the org structure, what's the biggest mistake people make?
zh: 在组织结构方面,人们犯的最大错误是什么?

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, I think it's actually, I'll give you a live one we're talking about right now.
